---
title: "Module 1 — LLM Application Architecture Patterns"
subtitle: "Day 1, hours 1–3 · theory, then the lab"
---

Most LLM products fail not because the model is weak but because the application
around it is unengineered: prompts concatenated inline with business logic, no
boundary between the app and the provider, an agent loop where a single call would
do, and no way to answer "what changed?" when quality drops.

This module gives you a pattern vocabulary and one architectural discipline —
**put the model behind a boundary** — so that structure, guards, evaluation and
cost all have somewhere to attach later in the week.

# Theory

## 1. LLM applications fail quietly

Classic software fails loudly: exceptions, 500s, red tests. LLM applications keep
returning 200s while the answers degrade.

| Failure mode | What it looks like | Fixed in |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-determinism** | The same input produces different output across calls, snapshots and providers. Anything downstream doing string matching is already broken. | M3 (validate), M5 (assert properties) |
| **Prompt drift** | A prompt edited casually in code silently changes behaviour for every user. The prompt *is* production logic. | M4 |
| **Silent quality decay** | A provider rotates a snapshot; accuracy drops six points; nobody notices for a month. | M5 |
| **Cost surprises** | A prompt edit doubles the bill and no code review flags it. | M6 |
| **New attack surface** | Users can *talk to* your logic. There is no parameterised-query equivalent. | M4 |
| **Provider coupling** | Written against one SDK, one model name, one price sheet. Procurement, residency rules and the market all change. | This module |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The five-minute exercise before any of this

Open a sixty-line "works on stage" chatbot — hardcoded model name, prompt inline,
no timeout, no state, `print` streaming — and list what breaks in production. A
room full of engineers finds most of the table above unprompted. Naming them
afterwards lands better than naming them first.
:::

## 2. Four patterns, as an escalation ladder

Each rung adds capability *and* cost, latency and failure surface. The
professional instinct is to stay as low as the use case allows.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    A["**Single call**<br/>one prompt → one response<br/>classification · extraction · single-turn Q&A"] --> B
    B["**Workflow / chain**<br/>fixed DAG: outline → draft → check<br/>multi-step, decomposition KNOWN"] --> C
    C["**Router**<br/>classify, then dispatch to specialists<br/>heterogeneous traffic"] --> D
    D["**Agentic loop**<br/>model chooses tools until done<br/>decomposition UNKNOWN at design time"]

    style A fill:#e8f4ea,stroke:#3c8d5a
    style B fill:#eef3fb,stroke:#4a76b8
    style C fill:#fdf3e3,stroke:#c78b2c
    style D fill:#fbeaea,stroke:#b84a4a
```

| Pattern | Cost/latency | Failure surface | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single call | 1× | smallest | classification, extraction, rewriting, single-turn Q&A |
| Workflow | n×, but predictable | per step, testable in isolation | multi-step tasks with a *known* decomposition |
| Router | 1 cheap + 1 handler | mis-routing, and it is measurable | heterogeneous traffic |
| Agentic loop | unbounded unless capped | largest: loops, tool misuse, runaway cost | you genuinely cannot enumerate the steps in advance |

Three points worth arguing about:

- **Workflows beat agents when the decomposition is known.** A fixed chain is
  testable step by step, has bounded cost, and fails locally. Start at the simplest
  pattern; escalate on evidence, not on vocabulary.
- **Routers are the workhorse.** Murshid's traffic is ~70% FAQ, ~25% transactional,
  ~5% escalation. Routing is what makes the economics work — and Module 6 turns
  that into a measured 91% cost reduction.
- **Agentic loops need governors:** max iterations, a token and spend budget, an
  allowed-tool list, and a human-readable trace. Murshid's tool loop (Module 3) is
  a *bounded* agentic loop — the course's only one, deliberately.

This is the diagram to keep open for the next four days.

```{mermaid}

    RT -->|service ~25%| SVC["service workflow<br/><small>+ bounded tool loop</small>"]
```

## 3. The model boundary

The single most consequential decision in an LLM application is where the model
boundary sits. The rule: **application code never imports a provider SDK.**

### Reading the contract

The whole boundary is one file. Here it is, in the order it matters — this is
`src/murshid/llm/interfaces.py`, not a simplification of it.

The **request** is what the application is allowed to ask for:

```python
class LLMRequest(BaseModel):
    messages: list[Message]
    model_alias: str = "murshid-default"  # resolved via config, never a literal model id
    temperature: float = Field(0.2, ge=0.0, le=2.0)
    max_tokens: int = Field(1024, gt=0)  # ALWAYS bounded
    tools: list[dict] | None = None       # provider-neutral JSON schema
    response_format: dict | None = None   # structured outputs (Module 3)
    cache_prefix_messages: int = 0        # how many leading messages are the stable prefix (M6)
```

Seven fields. `messages` is the obvious one; the other six are decisions this
course keeps coming back to:

- `model_alias` is a *name*, not an id. Nothing in the application ever writes
  `gpt-4o-2024-08-06`. The alias resolves through `configs/murshid.yaml`, which is
  why a provider swap is an environment variable rather than a search-and-replace.
- `max_tokens` has `gt=0` and a default. It cannot be `None`, so there is no path
  through this codebase that issues an unbounded generation. The architecture test
  enforces the same rule a second time, at the call site.
- `temperature` survives here even though the Anthropic Messages API no longer
  accepts it (Module 2). The normalised type keeps the union of what providers
  offer; each adapter drops what its own provider cannot take. Deleting the field
  to silence one adapter's `TypeError` would be the wrong repair.
- `tools` and `response_format` are provider-neutral JSON. Module 3 fills them.
- `cache_prefix_messages` is a Module 6 field sitting in a Module 1 file on
  purpose: prefix discipline is only cheap if the boundary was designed to carry it.

The **response** is what the application is allowed to learn:

```python
class Usage(BaseModel):
    input_tokens: int = 0
    output_tokens: int = 0
    cached_input_tokens: int = 0  # Module 6 pays close attention to this one


class LLMResponse(BaseModel):
    text: str | None = None
    tool_calls: list[ToolCall] = Field(default_factory=list)
    finish_reason: FinishReason = "stop"
    model_id: str = ""    # the CONCRETE model that answered, never the alias
    usage: Usage = Field(default_factory=Usage)
    latency_ms: float = 0.0
    route: str = ""       # which configured route served it (set by the client)
```

`model_id` and `route` are the two fields people leave out and regret. When an
answer is wrong, "which model, on which route, actually produced this?" is the
first question, and if the response cannot answer it the investigation starts with
guesswork. `usage` crossing the boundary is what makes Module 6's cost meter a
one-line change instead of a refactor — the meter reads a field that was already
there.

And the interface itself is four lines:

```python
@runtime_checkable
class LLMClient(Protocol):
    """Everything the application is allowed to know about a model provider."""

    def complete(self, request: LLMRequest) -> LLMResponse: ...
    def stream(self, request: LLMRequest) -> Iterator[StreamChunk]: ...
```

`Protocol` rather than a base class is deliberate: an adapter satisfies this by
having the right shape, with no import of ours and no inheritance. `FakeClient` in
the test suite is not a mock of the interface — it *is* an implementation, which is
why the same contract suite runs against it and against the live routes.

Three implementations sit behind it: `OpenAICompatClient` (which covers OpenAI
*and* vLLM *and* most gateways — the chat-completions schema is the de-facto wire
standard), `AnthropicClient`, and `FakeClient` for tests.

Finally, the error type, because failure has to cross the boundary in a normalised
shape too:

```python
class LLMError(RuntimeError):
    """Normalised provider failure. ``retryable`` drives Module 1's retry policy."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        message: str,
        *,
        status: int | None = None,
        retryable: bool = False,
        retry_after: float | None = None,
        raw: Any = None,
    ) -> None:
```

`retryable` is a *decision the adapter makes*, not a status code the retry loop
re-interprets. Each provider spells its failures differently; the adapter is where
that vocabulary is translated once, so the policy below can be written in terms of
one boolean instead of a growing table of status codes per provider.

- **Model names are configuration, not code.** `murshid-default` resolves through
  `configs/murshid.yaml` to a concrete id. Swapping providers, pinning a snapshot,
  or moving a route on-premise is a YAML edit and an environment variable.
- **The gateway layer** centralises keys, budgets, rate limiting, logging and
  failover. In Saudi enterprise practice it is often mandated — it is where PDPL
  logging controls and per-department cost attribution live. This classroom runs
  behind one, which is worth noticing: the classroom *is* the reference
  architecture.
- **What crosses the boundary:** a normalised request (messages, tools,
  response-format, parameters) and a normalised response (text, tool calls, finish
  reason, usage). Usage crossing the boundary is what makes Module 6's cost meter a
  one-line change rather than a refactor.

::: {.callout-important}
## This claim is tested, not asserted

`tests/test_architecture.py` walks the AST of every module under `src/murshid/`
and fails if anything outside `llm/openai_compat.py` and `llm/anthropic_client.py`
imports `openai` or `anthropic`. It also fails on an `LLMRequest` constructed
without `max_tokens`, and on prompt text inlined in Python.

A boundary that nothing checks is a boundary that lasts until the first deadline.
:::

## 4. State, streaming, and the sync/batch line

**LLM APIs are stateless.** Every request carries the whole conversation. "Memory"
is an application concern. Three strategies:

| Strategy | Cost per turn | Fails by | Murshid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full history | grows linearly, forever | context overflow mid-conversation, for your most engaged users first | rejected |
| **Windowed** (last k turns) | flat | forgetting turn 1 — visibly, predictably | **shipped**, k = 8 |
| Summarised | flat plus one cheap call | a summary that drops the fact that mattered | capstone extension |

**Context budget is an architectural constraint, not an afterthought.** History,
system prompt, retrieved content, tool schemas and output must fit — and cost
scales with all of it on *every* turn. Murshid's budget is written down in
[`docs/context_budget.md`](https://github.com/MohammadYusif/llm-application-engineering/blob/main/murshid/docs/context_budget.md);
you write your own in the lab below.

**Streaming is UX, not decoration.** A 500 ms time-to-first-token with streaming
*feels* faster than a four-second complete response at identical total latency.
Stream user-facing prose; do not stream machine-consumed structured output — you
cannot validate half a JSON object.

**Sync versus batch:** does a human wait for this response? No → batch candidate,
where provider batch APIs are typically half price and rate limits are kinder.

## 5. Reliability lives at the boundary, once

Provider APIs fail routinely: 429 rate limits, 500/529 overload, timeouts, and
content-filter refusals. Policy belongs in the adapter layer, in one file:

```python
# src/murshid/llm/resilient.py
ResilientClient(
    chain=[("primary", commercial), ("on_prem", vllm)],
    max_attempts=3,       # retries multiply cost and tail latency
    base_delay=1.0,       # exponential, jittered, Retry-After honoured
)
```

- **Timeouts always.** A hung LLM call with no timeout is a hung user.
- **Retry only what is retryable.** A malformed request retried three times is the
  same bug, three times slower, at three times the cost.
- **Fallback chains** end in a *degraded but honest* answer, never an error page —
  and the fallback hop gets evaluated too (Module 5), or failover becomes silent
  quality decay.
- **`max_tokens` always set**, per-conversation spend caps, and a circuit breaker
  that stops hammering a failing provider.

### Reading the retry loop

This is the whole of `ResilientClient.complete()`. Two nested loops — hops on the
outside, attempts on the inside — and every branch in it is a policy decision worth
stopping on.

```python
def complete(self, request: LLMRequest) -> LLMResponse:
    last_error: LLMError | None = None
    for hop_index, (hop_name, client) in enumerate(self._chain):
        for attempt in range(1, self._max_attempts + 1):
            self.attempts += 1
            try:
                response = client.complete(request)
            except LLMError as exc:
                last_error = exc
                if not exc.retryable:
                    log.warning("llm_not_retryable", hop=hop_name,
                                status=exc.status, error=type(exc).__name__)
                    break                      # a 400 is a bug: move on, do not hammer
                if attempt == self._max_attempts:
                    log.warning("llm_hop_exhausted", hop=hop_name, attempts=attempt)
                    break
                delay = self._delay_for(attempt, exc)
                log.warning("llm_retry", hop=hop_name, attempt=attempt,
                            status=exc.status, retry_after=exc.retry_after,
                            delay_s=round(delay, 2))
                self._sleep(delay)
            except Exception as exc:           # unknown failure: treat as non-retryable
                last_error = LLMError(str(exc), retryable=False, raw=exc)
                log.warning("llm_unexpected_error", hop=hop_name, error=type(exc).__name__)
                break
            else:
                if hop_index > 0:
                    self.fallbacks += 1
                    log.warning("fallback_served", hop=hop_name, model_id=response.model_id)
                return response
    raise AllHopsExhausted(f"all {len(self._chain)} model hops exhausted", ...)
```

Line by line, the parts that carry weight:

- **`if not exc.retryable: break`** — not `continue`. A non-retryable error means
  this request is malformed or unauthorised, so retrying it on *this* hop is
  pointless; the `break` drops to the next hop, where a different provider might
  disagree about whether the request is valid. Retrying a 400 three times is the
  same bug, three times slower, at three times the cost.
- **`except Exception` is a separate, non-retryable branch.** Anything the adapter
  did not normalise into an `LLMError` — a JSON decode failure, a bug in our own
  code — must not be retried, because a retry loop around a deterministic crash is
  an infinite loop with billing attached.
- **The `else` clause on the `try`** runs only when no exception was raised. It is
  the success path, and it is where the fallback counter increments: `hop_index > 0`
  is the definition of "we failed over", so `fallback_served` appears in the log
  exactly when it should and never when the primary answered.
- **`self._sleep` is injected** in the constructor (`sleep=time.sleep`). That is
  the only reason `tests/llm/test_resilient.py` can assert the backoff schedule
  without actually waiting eleven seconds. A hard-coded `time.sleep` here would make
  the retry policy untestable, and an untestable policy is one nobody changes with
  confidence.

The backoff itself is four lines, and the first of them is the one people miss:

```python
def _delay_for(self, attempt: int, error: LLMError) -> float:
    if error.retry_after is not None:          # honour the header before guessing
        return min(error.retry_after, self._max_delay)
    delay = self._base_delay * (2 ** (attempt - 1))
    return min(delay * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5), self._max_delay)   # jitter
```

The provider told you when to come back. Computing your own exponential backoff
while ignoring `Retry-After` is how a fleet of clients synchronises into a
thundering herd against a service that was trying to help. The jitter multiplier
exists for the same reason at a smaller scale: identical backoff across many
clients reproduces the spike it was meant to smooth.

### Streaming fails over on one condition

```python
for chunk in client.stream(request):
    emitted = emitted or bool(chunk.delta)
    yield chunk
...
except LLMError as exc:
    if emitted:
        raise
    continue                                    # nothing shown yet — try the next hop
```

Once a single token has reached the user, failing over would splice two different
models' answers into one paragraph. `emitted` is the whole guard: before the first
token, failover is invisible and correct; after it, the honest move is to surface
the failure and let the UI show its designed "generation failed" state.

And the last hop of every chain is not a model at all:

```python
def degraded_response(language: str = "en") -> LLMResponse:
    """The last hop of every chain: honest, cheap, and never an error page."""
```

It returns a bilingual sentence saying the service is temporarily unavailable and
pointing at the service centre. It costs nothing, it never fails, and it is the
difference between a citizen who tries again later and one who concludes the portal
is broken.

Run the drill rather than reading about it:

```bash
make drill-outage        # the primary model returns 529 for five minutes
make ask Q="How do I renew my commercial licence?"
# → llm_retry ... then fallback_served hop=fallback:vllm — the citizen never sees it
make drill-off
```

## 6. Common mistakes

1. **Agent-first design** for what is a router plus two workflows. Symptoms:
   unexplainable behaviour, unbounded cost, undebuggable traces.
2. **SDK calls sprinkled through business logic** — the provider migration that
   should be a config change becomes a six-week rewrite.
3. **No `max_tokens`, no timeout, no retry policy** — demo defaults that become
   production incidents.
4. **Unbounded conversation history** — cost grows per turn until the context
   overflows, in production, for the longest conversations first.
5. **Streaming everything**, including JSON meant for machines, which then gets
   "parsed" with a regex over partial chunks.
6. **Ignoring refusals as a response class.** Content-filter refusals are normal
   API behaviour and need designed UX, not a stack trace.

## Discussion

- Your product manager wants "an agent" because a competitor announced one. The
  traffic analysis says 78% FAQ. What do you build, and what do you tell them?
- The fallback model is 20% worse on Arabic. Is failing over still the right call?
  What evidence would settle it?
- Which single architectural decision in Murshid makes a data-residency
  requirement a routing policy instead of a rewrite?
